processing: Leaves and branches are boiled in an iron pot for about an hour and sun-dried, then repeatedly sprinkled with the hot boiling liquid and dried again. Japan's cultural agency classes it as unfermented, with no microbial stage, although some tea guides call it slightly fermented.
harvest_season: Summer: leaves grown on until then are cut with their branches and dried under the midsummer sun.
appearance_dry: Amber-coloured leaf and stem, tinted by the repeated coating of tea liquid.
appearance_liquor: Warm golden amber, a fair expectation from the leaf colour and method.
appearance_wet: Soft brownish leaf with pieces of stem, typical of boiled bancha.
taste_profile: Toasty and gentle, an easy everyday cup rather than a sharp or grassy one.

brewing.notes: Boiling water and a long steep suit it, as with other country banchas. It can also be simmered briefly in a kettle.

vintage_note: Sold as a summer-made country tea, usually from the most recent production, with no vintage culture around it. Only a couple of makers still follow the full traditional method, so ask whether the leaf was really boiled and basted in the sun. Low-caffeine claims come mainly from sellers and are not firmly established.
description:
Mimasaka Bancha is a summer bancha from the Mimasaka area of northern Okayama, and its method is a surprise: the leaf is boiled before it is ever dried.

Branches and leaves simmer for about an hour in an iron pot and dry in the sun. Then they get a basting of their own hot cooking liquid and go back into the sun, over and over. That coats the leaf in tea solids and gives it its amber colour.

The result is toasty and mild. Do not treat it like sencha: use plenty of boiling water and steep long.

It is sometimes described as fermented, and the region does make a separate fermented tea called gentoku-cha, so the two are worth keeping apart. Official description treats this bancha as unfermented, with the short sun-drying leaving no microbial stage. Look for makers who still follow the traditional process, since there are few of them.

It is a good next stop for anyone curious about Japan's rustic regional teas.
history:
Tea here is linked by tradition to the Nara-period temple Makiyama Chofuku-ji, though no surviving text fixes when growing began. A record from the Koan era of the Kamakura period mentions a tea field on the temple grounds, so organised tea-growing likely existed by then. The late Edo Emi Nōsho also describes tea-making in Mimasaka.

A local story claims the swordsman Miyamoto Musashi grew up drinking it, which is a legend and no more.

Production has shrunk sharply. In the Showa 30s, around 20 tea factories worked mainly in the Kaida district of Mimasaka city; now there are four, and only two companies keep making it in the traditional way.
